summary: Describes an RTP payload format for H.264 video, which is technically identical to ISO/IEC 14496-10. It allows packetizing one or more Network Abstraction Layer Units produced by an H.264 encoder. It was replaced by RFC 6184.

eli5.summary: It explains how to cut up a compressed video into small packages for sending over the Internet and put it back together at the other end.

questions: how is h.264 video sent over rtp
what are parameter sets in h.264
subtitle: How to send H.264 video over RTP for real-time communication.

tldr.problem: H.264 video encoders produce a stream of Network Abstraction Layer Units (NAL units) that need to be transmitted over RTP networks in video telephony, conferencing, and streaming applications.
tldr.mechanism: The payload format defines three ways to package NAL units into RTP packets: single NAL unit packets (one unit per packet), aggregation packets (multiple units with same or different timestamps), and fragmentation units (splitting a large unit across packets). Packetization modes support low-latency conversational use, streaming with packet reordering, and efficient transmission on constrained networks.
tldr.outcome: H.264 video can be reliably transmitted using RTP with support for various application requirements. RFC 6184 supersedes this specification.

today: RFC 3984 was the original RTP payload format for H.264 video. It was replaced by RFC 6184, which includes updates and additional guidance for H.264 RTP transmission.

sections.title: H.264 Video Coding
sections.content:
H.264 (also known as Advanced Video Coding or AVC) is a video compression standard that achieves significantly better compression than earlier standards like MPEG-2. The codec is divided into two layers: the Video Coding Layer (VCL), which handles the actual compression (transform, quantization, motion compensation, and filtering), and the Network Abstraction Layer (NAL), which wraps the VCL output into packets suitable for transmission.

The VCL encoder outputs slices—sequences of macroblocks with slice header information. The NAL encoder wraps these slices into NAL units, each consisting of a one-byte header and a payload. The NAL unit header indicates the unit type (which determines what kind of data it contains) and the reference importance (whether this unit affects future pictures). This design allows H.264 to work with diverse networks and applications, from low-bit-rate video telephony to high-definition broadcast.
sections.eli5: H.264 is a way to squeeze video down to a smaller size. The compression part makes the video smaller, and the packaging part wraps up the compressed pieces so they can travel over a network.

sections.title: NAL Units and Packetization Overview
sections.content:
A NAL unit consists of a header byte and payload data. The header byte breaks down as follows: a single forbidden-zero-bit (F), two bits indicating reference importance (NRI), and five bits indicating the NAL unit type. The type field tells the decoder what kind of data follows: slices (raw video), parameter sets (configuration data like picture size and coding modes), supplemental information (timestamps or recovery hints), or RTP-specific aggregation/fragmentation markers.

The RTP payload format defines three basic packet structures for sending NAL units: single NAL unit packets (each RTP packet contains exactly one NAL unit), aggregation packets (one RTP packet contains multiple NAL units, either with identical timestamps or with multiple timestamps), and fragmentation units (a single large NAL unit is split across multiple RTP packets).

The choice of packetization mode depends on the application. Single NAL unit mode is simple and suitable for low-latency applications that comply with ITU-T H.241. Non-interleaved mode allows aggregation and fragmentation but requires NAL units to be sent in their decoding order. Interleaved mode allows NAL units to be sent out of decoding order, enabling flexible reordering strategies for robustness.
sections.eli5: Video pieces are called NAL units. You can send them one per packet, bundle multiple pieces into one packet, or split a big piece across multiple packets. Different strategies work best for different situations.

sections.title: RTP Header and Timestamp Handling
sections.content:
The RTP header is used as follows: the marker bit (M) is set to 1 for the last RTP packet of an access unit (the last packet of a decoded picture), allowing efficient playout buffer management. The payload type is assigned dynamically or through profile negotiation. The sequence number is incremented for each packet and is used to determine NAL unit decoding order in single and non-interleaved modes.

The RTP timestamp is set to the sampling timestamp of the content using a 90 kHz clock rate. For single NAL unit packets, the timestamp represents when that NAL unit should be decoded. For aggregation packets combining NAL units with the same timestamp, the RTP timestamp is set to that common timestamp. For multi-time aggregation packets (which may contain NAL units with different presentation times), each aggregated NAL unit includes its own timestamp offset from the RTP header timestamp.

A critical aspect of H.264 support is that decoding order may differ from display order (due to B-frames that reference future pictures). The RTP timestamp reflects display time, while sequence numbers reflect transmission and (in some modes) decoding order.
sections.eli5: Each RTP packet has a timestamp saying when this video should be shown. A special bit marks the last packet of a complete picture. The packets are numbered so the receiver can put them back in the right order even if they arrive scrambled.

sections.title: RTP Payload Structures
sections.content:
Single NAL unit packets are the simplest: the RTP payload consists of a NAL unit header byte followed by the NAL unit payload. This is recommended for simple implementations and low-latency applications.

Aggregation packets bundle multiple NAL units into a single RTP packet to reduce overhead on networks with large packet sizes (like Ethernet). Two types of single-time aggregation packets (STAP-A and STAP-B) aggregate NAL units that all have the same timestamp. Multi-time aggregation packets (MTAP16 and MTAP24) aggregate NAL units with potentially different timestamps. Each aggregated NAL unit is preceded by a 16-bit size field, and MTAP variants include timestamp offsets (16 or 24 bits) for each unit.

Fragmentation units (FU-A and FU-B) split a single large NAL unit across multiple RTP packets when it exceeds the network MTU. An FU header indicates whether this is the start, middle, or end of a fragmented unit, and the original NAL unit type and reference importance are preserved. FU-B includes decoding order number information to support interleaved transmission.
sections.eli5: You can send video pieces three ways: one per packet, bundle a bunch into one packet (good for wired networks), or split a big piece across packets (necessary when packets are small).

sections.title: Parameter Sets and Decoding Configuration
sections.content:
H.264 uses two types of parameter sets—metadata that applies to many pictures or an entire coded video sequence. A sequence parameter set (SPS) contains information used throughout an entire coded video sequence: picture size, frame rate, level, chroma format, and the allowed set of quantization parameters. A picture parameter set (PPS) contains information used within a coded picture: entropy coding mode, slice group map, and other per-picture settings.

Each slice header includes a codeword identifying which SPS and PPS are active for that slice. This design allows an encoder and decoder to maintain multiple parameter sets simultaneously, enabling resolution or mode changes without synchronously updating all slices.

Parameter sets are sent as NAL units (types 7 and 8) and may be transmitted reliably out-of-band (before or separate from the video stream), in-band (within the RTP stream), or pre-configured by application design. The specification recommends sending parameter sets reliably and in advance of the slice data that depends on them, as parameter set loss would make recovery impossible without waiting for an IDR (instantaneous decoding refresh) picture.
sections.eli5: Compressed video also needs configuration data, like the size of the picture and what compression settings are in use. This data is sent separately from the picture data, and the decoder uses it to know how to decompress each picture.

sections.title: Decoding Order and Interleaved Transmission
sections.content:
H.264 supports out-of-order transmission of NAL units through the Decoding Order Number (DON), a 16-bit field included in certain packet types (STAP-B, MTAPs, and FU-B). DON allows a receiver to reorder packets to reconstruction proper NAL unit decoding order.

In single NAL unit mode, packets must be transmitted in decoding order (sequence numbers determine order). In non-interleaved mode, single NAL unit packets, STAP-As, and FU-As must be in decoding order, but STAP-B and MTAP packets may encode out-of-order transmission using DON. In interleaved mode, packets can be sent in any order, and DON is used to recover decoding order at the receiver.

Interleaved mode enables strategies like transmitting I-frame slices before dependent slices, or intelligently dropping less important pictures under congestion. However, it introduces complexity at both encoder and decoder. The specification includes detailed algorithms for recovering decoding order from DON values.
sections.eli5: Video can be sent in two ways: in the exact order the decoder needs (simple and fast), or jumbled in a smart way that the decoder can unsort. The jumbled approach is useful when network problems happen, because you can drop less important pieces and still decode what's left.

fields.name: F (Forbidden)
fields.desc: 0 = no errors, 1 = errors or syntax violations detected.

fields.name: NRI (Reference Importance)
fields.desc: 00 = discardable, 11 = most important. Indicates if unit is needed for reference pictures.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Indicates the NAL unit type: 1-23 for slices/data partitions, 24-29 for aggregation/fragmentation.
